title: A small fish
hook: govern a great country as you'd cook a small fish, without too much poking (Tao Te Ching 60)

segments.voice: Yesterday, frugal living, from chapter fifty-nine. Your line was frugal. What small thing did you keep back instead of spending? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

A small fish is sizzling in a pan. Someone stands over it with a spatula and can't leave it alone. Lift the edge. Check the color. Nudge it. Flip it. Flip it back. By the time it's cooked, it's in flakes all over the pan, and there isn't much fish left to serve. Chapter sixty of the Tao Te Ching takes that kitchen scene and sets it right next to a far bigger job: running a country. The comparison sounds like a joke. It isn't. Today, a small fish.
screen: `A FISH IN A HOT PAN.` → `FLIP, CHECK, FLIP AGAIN.` → `A COUNTRY IN THE SAME PAN.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. In James Legge's translation, chapter sixty opens: "Governing a great state is like cooking small fish." That's the whole instruction. It doesn't say how. It leaves the cook to work it out. Second, why a small fish. A thick cut of meat can take some handling. A small fish is delicate. An old commentary on the chapter, the one tradition credits to Heshang Gong, reads it this way: don't dare to stir it, or it falls apart. So the skill is mostly restraint. Get the heat right, put it in, and let it cook. A country, in this picture, is fragile in the same way. Every new order, every shake-up, every fresh rule turns the fish over one more time. Third, the chapter's stranger second half. It says that when the world is ruled by the Tao, the spirits of the dead lose their power to harm. Not that they have no power, the chapter adds, but that it doesn't hurt people. And the sage doesn't hurt people either. When neither side does harm, their goodness flows together. Readers take this in different ways. Some hear old beliefs about ghosts. Some hear that a calm, unmeddling order leaves less room for dread of any kind. The text doesn't settle it. Fourth, closer to home. Daily life has its own small fish: an inbox, a team, a teenager's homework, a sourdough starter, a friendship that went quiet. And the pull is to keep turning it. One more text. One more check. One more tweak to the plan. Chapter sixty leaves a plain kitchen question on the counter. Is this still cooking, or is it just poking?
screen: `A GREAT STATE, A SMALL FISH.` · `EVERY TURN BREAKS IT A LITTLE.` · `SPIRITS THAT DO NO HARM.` · then, large: `COOKING, OR JUST POKING?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop fussing with one thing. Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one thing you've been turning over and over. A message you keep rereading. A plan you keep adjusting. A person you keep checking on. Notice the hand reaching for the spatula again. Now, for these two minutes, set the spatula down. The fish is in the pan. The heat is on. Nothing needs your hand right now. If the urge to check comes back, notice it, and let it drift off like steam rising from the pan. The bell holds the time.
A small fish. In chapter sixty, ruling a great state is like cooking one: handle it lightly, or it falls apart. Today's word.
Your line: don't poke. Pick one thing today you'd normally keep adjusting, and leave it alone until it's done. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty as advice for anyone in charge of something fragile: set it up well, then hold back from constant meddling.

notes: Check the Legge 1891 quotation of chapter 60 word for word.
The Heshang Gong commentary paraphrase (烹小鮮…不敢撓，恐其糜也) should be checked against the received commentary; the attribution to Heshang Gong is traditional, hence 'the one tradition credits to'.
The index hook's 'without too much poking' is the commentary's reading, not words in the chapter; the script says so.
Original 治大國若烹小鮮 (zhì dà guó ruò pēng xiǎo xiān) rendered as an approximate English sound; confirm.
